author: Rahul kp
title: Company vs
simple_words: A company is a separate person in law. A partnership firm is just the partners together.

definitions.meaning: An artificial person formed and registered under the Companies Act, with its own separate legal identity from its members.
Relation between persons who agree to share profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.

key_points: A company has a ==separate legal entity==; a firm has none apart from its partners.
Members of a limited company have ==limited liability==; partners have unlimited, joint and several liability.
A company has ==perpetual succession==; a firm is affected by death or retirement of a partner unless agreed otherwise.
!!Registration is compulsory for a company!!; for a firm it is optional.

insight.text: A company can own property, sue and be sued in its own name, but a firm acts through its partners.

memory_trick.explanation: Company wears a cloak: members hide behind it, so liability is limited and it never dies. Firm has no cloak: partners stand bare and exposed.

steps: Check: is it registered as company?
exam_tip: In MCQs, a statement saying a firm is a separate legal entity from its partners is false under the Partnership Act. Check the word 'separate'.

doubt.question: Do all companies have limited liability?
doubt.answer: No. An unlimited company exists too, but a company limited by shares or guarantee limits member liability. The separate entity status stays in all cases.

mistakes.wrong: A firm is a separate legal entity like a company
mistakes.right: Under the Partnership Act, a firm is not separate from its partners; a company is separate.

mistakes.wrong: Partners have limited liability like shareholders
mistakes.right: Partners of a general partnership have unlimited, joint and several liability for firm debts.

mistakes.wrong: Registration of a firm is compulsory
mistakes.right: Firm registration is optional, though unregistered firms face disabilities in suing. Company registration is compulsory.

mistakes.wrong: Death of a member ends a company
mistakes.right: A company has perpetual succession; membership changes do not end it.

Checker 1: trick_hook says 'remember with LAPPS', but the memory trick is 'Corporate Cloak' and LAPPS is never explained. LAPPS also does not match the table rows (Legal entity, Liability, Succession, Registration, Governing law). Fix: change the hook to the Cloak trick, or use an acronym that matches the five rows.

Checker 1: Insight punchline 'Company sues; partners sue together!' oversimplifies. Under Order XXX CPC, partners may sue or be sued in the firm name, and a registered firm can sue third parties (s. 69). Suggested wording: 'A company sues in its own right; a firm's suit in the firm name is really a suit by all the partners.'

Checker 1: Memory trick explanation: 'members hide behind it, so liability is limited and it never dies' is too absolute. Unlimited companies exist (as the doubt answer itself says), and a company can end through winding up or striking off. Suggested wording: 'liability can be limited, and the company does not die when a member dies or leaves; it ends only by a legal process.'

Checker 2: trick_hook says 'remember with LAPPS', but the memory trick given is 'Company = Corporate Cloak', and LAPPS is never explained. Make the two match. Either give a LAPPS expansion that covers the 5 table rows (Legal entity, Act, Perpetual succession, Personal liability, Registration), or change the hook to match the Cloak trick. The Cloak trick also covers only liability and succession, not all 5 rows.

Checker 2: Insight punchline 'Company sues; partners sue together!' is loose wording. A registered firm sues in the firm's name through its partners, and an unregistered firm is barred by S.69. It is better to say 'Company sues in its own name; a firm sues through its partners'.
